title: Don't call me God
hookLine: he says whoever calls him God will fall; he is only the servant of the Supreme (Bachitar Natak 6)

cards: Fans can get carried away. A singer, a coach, a preacher, a founder: first they're admired, then adored, and before long people are saying things about them that no human being should hear. Some leaders enjoy it.
Some quietly let it grow. In Bachitar Natak, the tenth Guru sees this coming. He has just told how he was sent into the world.
And right there, before anyone can get carried away, he draws a hard line.

teach.h: WHOEVER CALLS ME GOD WILL FALL.
teach.b: Here are the lines, in paraphrase. Whoever calls me the Supreme Lord will fall into the pit of hell.
Know me as His servant, and have no doubt about it.

teach.h: IN THE PLAY, NOT ITS AUTHOR.
teach.b: I am the servant of the Supreme Being, and I have come to see the play of the world. Three things stand out. First, the warning isn't soft.
He doesn't say, please don't. He says the one who calls him God will fall. The danger he names isn't to his reputation; it's to the person who makes the mistake.
Second, the word he chooses for himself: das, servant. Not a modest title for a great man, but the plain word for someone who serves.
The Guru of the Sikhs, the leader of the Khalsa, and his name for himself in his own life story is the servant of the Supreme. Third, it fits yesterday.
He came, he says, to see the play of the world: tamasha, a spectacle, a show. The servant is in the play. He's not the playwright.
Sikhs hold the Guru in deep reverence, and they also hold this line close. The Gurus are honored as the ones who carry God's word, and God alone is worshiped.

Guru Gobind Singh writes that boundary into his own story so nobody can blur it later. In the same passage, he adds that he speaks what the Lord tells him to speak, and he does not keep quiet out of fear of anyone.

teach.h: HUMBLE ABOUT HIMSELF, BOLD IN HIS WORD.
teach.b: Humble about who he is, bold about what he's been given to say, both at once.

how: Sikhs quote these lines from Bachitar Natak to show that the Gurus are revered as messengers of the divine word while God alone is worshiped.

games.q: what does “don't call me god” mean?
o: a plea to stop swearing oaths in God's name
a rule against saying God's name out loud
the Guru's warning: he is God's servant, not God

games.q: the Guru's line, piece by piece: tap the pairs.

s: Guru Gobind Singh asked to be worshiped as God
he warns that whoever calls him the Supreme Lord will fall.
he calls himself the servant of the Supreme in his own life story
know me as His servant, he says, come to see the play of the world.
his humility made him quiet about what he'd been given to say
he says he speaks what the Lord tells him, and doesn't keep quiet out of fear.

games.q: you've just written that you were sent into the world by God. people will be tempted to worship you. what do you write next?
o: whoever calls me God will fall; know me as His servant.
games.why: Guru Gobind Singh writes the boundary into his own story so no one can blur it later.

practice: Bring to mind something you've done that you're proud of, a meal, a kid you helped raise, a hard thing you finished, and let the pride be there.

Then trace what made it possible, the teachers, the hands before yours, the breath you didn't make, and let some of the credit travel to them and, if this is your way, to the One. If you pray, rest in Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Don't call me God. The tenth Guru's own line: whoever calls me the Supreme will fall; know me as His servant, come to see the play of the world. Today's word.

orig.note: servant: the word the tenth Guru uses for himself in Bachitar Natak.

carryVoice: Your line: only the servant. In the play, not the playwright. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Dasam Granth, Bachitar Natak, chapter 6 (jo ham ko parmesar uchar hai, te sabh narak kund mahi par hai; mai ho param purakh ko dasa, dekhan aio jagat tamasa)
